answer.rationale: Timeline is the strongest signal available: the release landed ~2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing ~90m ago, so the release is the leading suspect and rollback is the only candidate that addresses a suspected cause rather than masking a symptom. Critically, memory_b2 carries an explicit carve-out — never fail over while writes are hot — and settlement traffic is at daily peak with heavy writes, so regional_failover is disqualified outright despite its attractive headline ('latency recovered within minutes'); that memory is exactly the kind whose summary reads better than its caveat, which is why I want its original record. add_capacity (b3) was validated against a queue-depth/throughput surge, not a post-release latency regression, and provisioning is slow relative to a 90-minute-and-worsening curve. enable_circuit_breaker (b4) was validated against an external partner outage; there is no evidence of a dependency failure here, and failing fast on our own write path during settlement peak would shed customer writes — directly against the primary objective. route_read_replicas (b5) helped a read-heavy dashboard contend with the primary; this is a write-path problem, so it is the wrong mechanism. I verify memory_b1 because it is the memory I am actually acting on and its summary is suspiciously clean ('without customer impact') — I need to know whether that rollback happened at low traffic rather than at settlement peak, since rollback safety during hot writes is the entire question. I verify memory_b2 not because I intend to fail over but because its caveat is the constraint ruling out the fastest-looking option; if the original record shows the write-loss condition was narrower than remembered, my option set changes. Scale is a small guarded test: memory_b6 establishes that staged cohorts here surface regressions inside an hour, so I roll back a canary cohort first and watch write-path p99 and replication lag before widening. This preserves the causal uncertainty — if the release is not the cause, a broad rollback during peak settlement would be a large write-risking change made on a correlation, and I would have spent my one intervention. Risks I am carrying explicitly: the correlation may be coincidental (an organic settlement-peak saturation would look similar), rollback itself touches the write path during heavy writes and could drop in-flight transactions, and all these memories are 12-56 days stale against a system that has since changed.
